citation.title: Using Imperfect Surrogates for Downstream Inference: Design-based Supervised Learning for Social Science Applications of Large Language Models
citation.venue_or_publisher: 37th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2023)
citation.type: conference paper (main text, 13 pages including references; supplement is a separate file and not in the text)

question: How to use imperfect labels produced by large language models (surrogates) in later statistical analyses, such as regressions, without bias and with valid confidence intervals, by combining them with a smaller number of expert (gold-standard) labels.
data: Simulations and tests on 18 datasets. (1) Congressional Bills Project: 10K bills drawn at random (the outcome is whether a bill is labelled Macroeconomy), GPT-3 zero-shot labels (accuracy 68% balanced, 90% imbalanced), 500 simulations per point, gold-standard samples of 100 to 1000. (2) 17 classification datasets from Ziems et al. (2023), labelled with flan-ul2, with n = 100 gold-standard labels in the reported table (9 of the 17 shown; the remaining 8 are in the supplement, which is not in the file). None of the data concern business, fossil fuels, climate or participant lists.
method: Design-based supervised learning (DSL). Every document gets a surrogate label (for example from an LLM). A random or stratified sample, with a known and non-zero probability, is labelled by experts. A prediction model is fitted on the expert labels with K-fold cross-fitting, a bias-corrected pseudo-outcome is built, and the downstream regression uses that pseudo-outcome. Compared with surrogate-only (SO), gold-standard-only (GSO) and conventional supervised learning (SL) on bias, coverage of 95% confidence intervals and root mean squared error (RMSE).

definitions.definition: Scalable but error-prone labels, for example produced by an LLM, used in place of expert labels.
definitions.quote: We call these more scalable—but error-prone—labels, surrogate labels.

definitions.definition: Labels produced by expert annotation for a subset of documents.
definitions.quote: We assume the outcome is costly to measure and we can choose to have an expert annotate a subset of the documents to provide the gold-standard Y.

definitions.definition: The unknown and varying mismatch between the gold-standard label and the surrogate.
definitions.quote: measurement error—the unknown and heterogeneous mismatch between the gold-standard label and the surrogate

definitions.definition: The researcher controls and knows the probability with which each document is sampled for gold-standard labelling, and that probability is above zero (Assumption 1).
definitions.quote: The assumption holds when the researcher directly controls the sampling design.

proxies.concept: True class of a document (the gold standard)
proxies.indicator: Expert annotation of a sampled subset of documents.
proxies.quote: We assume the outcome is costly to measure and we can choose to have an expert annotate a subset of the documents to provide the gold-standard Y.

proxies.concept: Class of every document, at scale
proxies.indicator: LLM annotation used as a surrogate label.
proxies.quote: Q represent surrogate labels (e.g. from an LLM).

findings.claim: Using LLM labels directly in a downstream regression gives biased estimates and invalid confidence intervals, even when the LLM is 80-90% accurate (authors' simulation).
findings.quote: We show that direct use of surrogate labels in downstream statistical analyses leads to substantial bias and invalid confidence intervals, even with high surrogate accuracy of 80–90%.

findings.claim: In a simulated example with 90% surrogate accuracy, a nominal 95% confidence interval covered the truth only 40% of the time.
findings.quote: even with surrogate accuracy of 90%, the bias is substantial and the coverage of a 95% confidence interval is only 40% in downstream regression.

findings.claim: On the Congressional Bills data, DSL had lower error than using gold-standard labels alone (14% RMSE gain in the balanced zero-shot condition).
findings.quote: DSL achieves a 14% gain in RMSE over GSO (balanced condition) as shown in Figure 3.

findings.claim: On 17 benchmark classification tasks, surrogate-only estimates of class shares were biased with poor coverage even when LLM accuracy was above 70%; DSL with 100 expert labels had low bias and near-nominal coverage.
findings.quote: Even for surrogate labels above 70% accuracy, the SO estimator has high bias and consequentially poor coverage for this aggregate quantity.

limitations.point: DSL is built for one setting: a downstream regression (or similar estimate) on labels for a corpus that is available from the start. It does not give individual document classifications.
limitations.quote: First, DSL is focused on a very specific setting: outcome variables used in a regression where researchers need to annotate a corpus of documents available from the outset.

limitations.point: The method needs accurate gold-standard labels, which may be hard to get.
limitations.quote: Like any method using gold-standard labels, DSL can be sensitive to the gold-standard being accurate

limitations.point: DSL favours low bias and valid coverage over prediction error; where RMSE is the main goal, conventional supervised learning may be better.
limitations.quote: As SL explicitly targets RMSE, it may be the better option if that is the primary consideration.

limitations.point: The file holds the main paper only. The supplement (extra results, other sample sizes, five-shot experiments, proofs, the 8 remaining benchmark tasks) is a separate document and was not read.

The paper does not test classification of organisations, business or fossil-fuel linkage, or any list of participants. Its evidence comes from bill topics and other text benchmarks, so applicability to organisation classification is not shown in the text.
